newsitem.title: UK: Britain's Major loses parliamentary majority.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Major loses parliamentary majority.

text.p: Britain's opposition Labour Party scored a decisive victory in a parliamentary by-election, robbing Prime Minister John Major of his majority in the House of Commons on Friday.

Labour's triumph on Thursday night in the Barnsley East constituency in northern England -- one of its strongholds -- was the latest blow to Major's Conservative Party, already deeply divided over relations with Europe and trailing badly in opinion polls.
The result means the Conservatives have lost their parliamentary majority for the first time since Major's predecessor Margaret Thatcher took power 17 years ago.
Labour local council leader Jeff Ennis won 13,683 votes against 1,299 for Conservative Jane Ellison, who finished third behind Liberal Democrat David Willis with 1,502.

Ennis was defending a Labour majority of 24,777 votes won by his predecessor Terry Patchett, whose recent death led to the by-election. While Barnsley East was vacant, Labour and other opposition parties were, until Ennis's victory, still one short of the Conservatives' 323 seats in parliament.

Barnsley East was one of the last tests of public opinion before the next general election -- which must be called by next May -- but the run-down, working-class constituency has long voted left of centre and is not typical of the nation at large.
Local activists say the constituency is usually one where the Labour vote is not counted but weighed, although Thursday's turnout was a low 33 percent of the 53,000 electorate.
"Tonight's result in Barnsley East should be seen as a springboard to Labour victory in a general election," said Ennis.
Labour Party leader Tony Blair said: "The government majority has gone and we will continue to pile on the pressure until the government has gone too."

But if Labour was rejoicing at the by-election victory, the party was facing deep embarrassment over an allegation that one of its "spin doctors" had attempted to rig a BBC radio listeners' poll to find the year's most influential figure.
The BBC said it had discovered "an organised attempt" by the Labour worker to rig the ballot by persuading fellow party members to send in thousands of votes on behalf of Blair.
A leaked Labour memo said these votes could be sent in by fax "though preferably not on fax machines which identify the sender as the Labour Party".
An embarrassed Blair said: "I know absolutely nothing about this."
Even senior Conservatives acknowledged that the electoral prospects for the party were now grim.

Former party deputy chairman Lord Archer said: "If we go into the next general election as divided as we are today we will lose and we will deserve to lose. If we don't pull together we will be beaten."

Despite the loss of the government's majority, Labour has made clear it will not move immediately to a confidence vote in parliament, where Major can count on the support of nine pro-British Ulster Unionists from Northern Ireland.
The result nevertheless deepened Major's problems, coming days after he effectively lost his majority in parliament when a disgruntled Conservative legislator, Sir John Gorst, withdrew support.
Even if Gorst is still formally counted as a Conservative, the party's 323 voting members of parliament are now evenly matched by legislators sitting for opposition parties.
